public_glossary.card_definition: It is a narrower thing than the word usually implies. An audit compares an account against a record, so it catches an action reported but not taken, or taken and not reported. Whether the action was a good idea is a separate question the audit does not touch.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This is the check most systems lack, because a component's own summary is normally the only account of what it did, and it is written by the thing under examination.
public_glossary.example: The closeout faithfulness audit compares a session's report against its trace.
public_glossary.label: audit
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An audit here is a check of whether a report matches what actually happened, rather than a check of whether the work itself was correct.
public_glossary.reader_rule: An audit tells you whether a report was faithful, not whether the work was right.
public_glossary.scope_note: An audit establishes the agreement between a report and a record.
public_glossary.short_definition: An audit here is a check of whether a report matches what actually happened, rather than a check of whether the work itself was correct.

public_glossary.card_definition: Authority is always scoped: a registry may own an identifier, a theorem checker may settle proof validity, and an operator may authorize publication. None of those roles automatically owns the others.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A useful system keeps authority close to the artifact that can actually maintain the fact and prevents summaries or generated views from silently inheriting it.
public_glossary.example: The term registry is authoritative for glossary membership, while the generated glossary page is not.
public_glossary.label: authority
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Confidence, prominence, or repetition does not create authority.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Authority is the recognized right of a particular source, rule, or actor to settle a stated kind of fact or permit a stated action.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask who or what is allowed to settle this exact question before treating a statement as final.
public_glossary.scope_note: Authority covers the decision class, artifact, time, and conditions named by its governing contract.
public_glossary.short_definition: Authority is the recognized right of a particular source, rule, or actor to settle a stated kind of fact or permit a stated action.

public_glossary.card_definition: The doctrine is layered: axioms at the top, then principles, then standards and skills below them. An axiom is a formal declaration that holds across every context the system operates in, such as voice authority, projection discipline, or operator scope. A principle is derived from an axiom and judged against it in a bounded setting, whereas the axiom is the fixed point the rest of the lattice composes against. The system targets roughly seven such axioms, and they remain provisional.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An axiom relates to a principle the way a mathematical axiom relates to a theorem: the principle is derived and judged against the axiom, while the axiom is taken as given. A well-chosen axiom makes the principles and standards beneath it easier to derive, because it captures a single design intuition the whole system holds constant.
public_glossary.example: AX-7, "Typed partiality and refusal", is a concrete axiom: it fixes how the system represents incomplete knowledge and when it must decline rather than guess, an invariant every lower rule is built to respect.

example_route.gloss: open one axiom in the doctrine lattice
example_route.label: Typed partiality and refusal

public_glossary.label: axiom
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An ai_workflow axiom is a promoted system constraint. It is not automatically a mathematical axiom, self-evident truth, or externally accepted principle.
public_glossary.non_example: An axiom is not a style preference, a goal, or a feature of the product. It is also not the same as a principle: a principle is a derived rule applied in context, whereas an axiom is the underived constraint that principle is measured against.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An axiom is a primitive, non-derived constraint the system treats as always binding, sitting above the principles that interpret it into behaviour for particular situations.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read an axiom as the strongest, most general commitment on the page: if a lower rule appears to conflict with it, the axiom is what holds. It states an invariant, not a procedure.

relationships.gloss: Axioms constrain the principle layer.
Axioms are the upper doctrine layer.
Axioms are the root of the governance lattice.

public_glossary.scope_note: Axioms appear in the doctrine and the rules-and-ideas reference, where they form the top tier of the lattice above principles, standards, and skills. There are about seven, and they govern invariants such as voice authority, projection discipline, lattice connectivity, operator scope, and primitive choice.
public_glossary.short_definition: An axiom is a primitive, non-derived constraint the system treats as always binding, sitting above the principles that interpret it into behaviour for particular situations.

source_refs.gloss: PD4 lattice layer description.
Governance lattice discussion names the axiom layer.
Root ontology places axioms above principles.

public_glossary.card_definition: Most of what is published here is backend. That is not an accident of scope, it is where the checkable claims live: a screen is demonstrated, whereas a routine that reads an input and writes a result can be run by anyone and compared.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The asymmetry explains the shape of the release. What could be given away as evidence was given away; what could only be shown was recorded instead.
public_glossary.example: The components are backend machinery; the frontend appears only in the videos.
public_glossary.label: backend
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The backend is the machinery a system runs on: the processing, storage and logic behind whatever a person sees.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Backend claims are the ones you can test yourself. Weigh them accordingly.
public_glossary.scope_note: Published backend components establish their own behaviour on their own inputs.
public_glossary.short_definition: The backend is the machinery a system runs on: the processing, storage and logic behind whatever a person sees.

public_glossary.card_definition: Many records on this site are written as a ladder of bands rather than a single block of text: word, phrase, flag, card, context, deep, and evidence, depending on the profile. The same item is available at each band, and the bands sit one inside the next like a telescope or a set of nested dolls, so a short browse can open into a working summary and then into full detail. A band is governed by a contract, not by a word count, so what appears at each level is fixed by rule rather than by how much someone happened to write.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The depth ladder belongs to a compression profile, which declares the full set of bands and what each one must hold; an individual record then fills those bands in. This is why a description can be expanded or collapsed in a predictable way, and why drift is flagged against one specific band rather than the whole file.
public_glossary.example: The doctrine reference entry that presents a standard as a schema contract with an explicit scope limit is one band in action: a single fixed level of description that states exactly what it covers and what it does not.

example_route.gloss: open one entry written at a single fixed band
example_route.label: standard as schema contract with explicit scope limit

public_glossary.label: band
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Band means a level in the repository's compression ladder, not a frequency band, musical group, statistical interval, or general taxonomy level.
public_glossary.non_example: A band is not a paragraph length or a writing style, and it is not the whole record. It is one defined level of a depth ladder, with a contract for what that level must contain.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A band is a named, schema-governed level of descriptive depth—from a one-word signal to full evidence—that fixes what a compressed view must include, may omit, and must point to next.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A band tells you the depth of what you are reading, not just its length. If a band does not answer your question, follow it down to the next band rather than assuming the detail is absent.

relationships.gloss: A compression profile declares its legal bands and band contracts.
Bands are how an affordance row shows itself at different costs.
Hologram nodes render rows through a requested band.

public_glossary.scope_note: Bands appear wherever the site offers a thing at more than one depth: component and paper-module summaries that expand, doctrine cards, and the layered entries in the doctrine reference. The vocabulary comes from the compression profiles and the navigation design that the public pages are generated from.
public_glossary.short_definition: A band is a named, schema-governed level of descriptive depth—from a one-word signal to full evidence—that fixes what a compressed view must include, may omit, and must point to next.

source_refs.gloss: Bands-as-schemas refinement.
System-term band contract.

public_glossary.card_definition: Barriers are the most useful negative results and the easiest to overstate. One that closes two approaches can read as closing the subject, and the difference matters entirely: an approach still open after a barrier is where the remaining work is. Every barrier recorded here is required to state what it does not rule out.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This requirement came from a real error rather than from caution. A parity obstruction was carried to the edge of publication as closing the certificate engines for one problem; a third, weaker engine in the same file was untouched by it and was found by accident. No surface recorded which engines existed, so nothing could have caught it.
public_glossary.example: 61 relations in the map record a barrier, each carrying a mandatory statement of what it fails to rule out.
public_glossary.label: barrier
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A barrier is a proved result showing that a particular route to a problem cannot work, closing off an approach rather than advancing towards a solution.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For any barrier, read what it leaves open. That is the part that decides what to do next.
public_glossary.scope_note: A barrier establishes that one route fails. It says nothing about routes it does not name.
public_glossary.short_definition: A barrier is a proved result showing that a particular route to a problem cannot work, closing off an approach rather than advancing towards a solution.

public_glossary.card_definition: Base two gives powers 2, 4, 8, and so on, while base three-halves gives rational powers. Changing the base can change the arithmetic enough that a theorem at one base says little about another.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Integer bases support ordinary positional digit expansions, while rational bases introduce extra denominator structure that can defeat arguments built for whole-number bases.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #1049 studies a Lambert-type series at rational bases, with three-halves as the smallest resistant explicit case.
public_glossary.label: base
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Base here does not mean a database, code superclass, or physical support.
public_glossary.reader_preview: In these papers, a base is the number whose successive powers organize a numeral expansion or appear in the denominators of a series.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check which base a series or digit argument uses before transferring a result.
public_glossary.scope_note: Base covers the explicitly named numeral or exponential base in one series, expansion, or theorem.
public_glossary.short_definition: In these papers, a base is the number whose successive powers organize a numeral expansion or appear in the denominators of a series.

public_glossary.card_definition: A benchmark makes comparison possible only inside its declared design. Its usefulness depends on representative tasks, protected answers, honest scoring, and resistance to leakage or gaming; a benchmark score is never a general measure of intelligence or safety.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Benchmarks are measurement instruments whose validity can drift when systems train on the test set, optimize to the metric, or exploit quirks that do not transfer to the intended real-world task.
public_glossary.example: A premise-retrieval benchmark can compare which relevant lemmas different search methods return for the same queries.
public_glossary.label: benchmark
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A single impressive demo or hand-picked example is not a benchmark.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A benchmark is a fixed set of tasks, inputs, metrics, and scoring rules used to compare performance under repeatable conditions.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a benchmark result together with its task set, metric, baseline, and leakage controls.
public_glossary.scope_note: A benchmark covers the declared tasks, data, metric, model or system version, and execution conditions.
public_glossary.short_definition: A benchmark is a fixed set of tasks, inputs, metrics, and scoring rules used to compare performance under repeatable conditions.

public_glossary.card_definition: For numbers between zero and one, the digits appear after the binary point just as decimal digits appear after a decimal point. A rational number has an eventually repeating expansion, which turns some irrationality questions into questions about whether repetition is possible.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Finite computation can reveal a long prefix but cannot prove that no repeating tail ever begins, so digit evidence alone does not establish irrationality.
public_glossary.example: The binary totient series is studied through constraints that rationality would impose on its eventual binary digits.
public_glossary.label: binary expansion
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A decimal approximation printed with zeros and ones is not automatically a binary expansion.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A binary expansion is a representation of a number using powers of two and digits limited to zero and one.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When an argument uses binary digits, ask whether it concerns the exact infinite expansion or only a computed prefix.
public_glossary.scope_note: A binary expansion covers one number under the standard base-two representation convention.
public_glossary.short_definition: A binary expansion is a representation of a number using powers of two and digits limited to zero and one.

public_glossary.card_definition: A binding is stronger than mentioning two things in the same paragraph. It names the relationship, identifies both sides, and makes the connection inspectable so later work can detect when one side changes or disappears.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Bindings turn an implied association into system state: evidence can bind to a claim, a path can bind to an artifact, and a status can bind to the actions it permits.
public_glossary.example: A result record binds a check's outcome to the exact input and source revision that produced it.
public_glossary.label: bind
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Two terms appearing near each other are not bound unless a relationship between them is explicitly recorded.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To bind two things is to record an explicit connection that later readers or checks are expected to preserve and follow.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When text says one object binds another, look for the recorded relationship and the rule that depends on it.
public_glossary.scope_note: A binding covers the named relationship between its declared endpoints, not every possible relation between those objects.
public_glossary.short_definition: To bind two things is to record an explicit connection that later readers or checks are expected to preserve and follow.

public_glossary.card_definition: A blocker should be actionable or at least observable: it identifies what cannot happen, why, and what change would permit progress. Delay or difficulty alone does not necessarily constitute a block.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Blocks are scoped to paths through a process; an alternative safe route may remain open even when one path is blocked.
public_glossary.example: A missing required source file blocks a builder that cannot produce a truthful projection without it.
public_glossary.label: blocked
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A slow test is not blocked while it is still making expected progress.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Blocked describes work or movement that cannot proceed because a named condition, dependency, permission, or obstacle prevents it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is blocked, verify the blocking condition and the exact re-entry condition rather than assuming the whole task is impossible.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers dependency, permission, validation, resource, and coordination obstacles.
public_glossary.short_definition: Blocked describes work or movement that cannot proceed because a named condition, dependency, permission, or obstacle prevents it.

public_glossary.card_definition: Boards turn many records into an at-a-glance operational view. They are usually projections over underlying data, so freshness and update ownership determine how much reliance they deserve.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A board can coordinate action without becoming the source authority for every item it displays.
public_glossary.example: A prediction-market board displays contracts, prices, and status for comparison.
public_glossary.label: board
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A decorative grid of cards is not an operational board if it carries no shared state or choices.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A board is a shared visual or structured surface that organizes items, status, decisions, or controls for collective inspection.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a board to orient and select items, then follow its routes to the owning records for exact evidence.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers dashboards, task boards, market boards, and control-room projections.
public_glossary.short_definition: A board is a shared visual or structured surface that organizes items, status, decisions, or controls for collective inspection.

public_glossary.card_definition: The body carries what a reader is meant to read in full. Titles, menus, summaries, and indexes may point to a body without duplicating it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Separating body content from navigation and metadata lets the site package, search, and deduplicate long texts without treating every presentation as a second copy.
public_glossary.example: A paper module page carries the module's body, while a component card carries only a synopsis and route.
public_glossary.label: body
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A heading, search result, or metadata row is not the document body.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A body is the main substantive content of a document, page, paper, or record, excluding its surrounding navigation and metadata.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Follow the body pointer when a synopsis is too compressed to support the claim you need.
public_glossary.scope_note: Body covers the content region declared as the complete reading text for one artifact.
public_glossary.short_definition: A body is the main substantive content of a document, page, paper, or record, excluding its surrounding navigation and metadata.

public_glossary.card_definition: Bounds are how finite work says something about an infinite question. Checking every case is impossible; proving that any failure must occur beyond a certain point, and then checking everything below it, is not. Much of the computation here has that shape.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The useful bounds are the sharp ones. A bound that leaves an infinite region unexamined converts a problem into a smaller problem rather than closing it.
public_glossary.example: Every rational value of the binary totient series is excluded up to a sharp 240-binary-digit bound.
public_glossary.label: bound
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A bound is a limit past which a quantity is shown not to go, in one direction or the other.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A bound tells you where something cannot be. Whether the remaining region is searchable is a separate question.
public_glossary.scope_note: A bound covers the quantity and range it is proved for.
public_glossary.short_definition: A bound is a limit past which a quantity is shown not to go, in one direction or the other.

public_glossary.card_definition: A bridge carries one prompt packet out to an external worker, such as a separate reasoning model or research run, and carries one response packet back. The worker sees only what the controlling lane chose to send, and the response returns as candidate evidence that the owning lane then validates, imports, or discards. The same packet can be sent to many workers in parallel, which is what makes a bridge useful for research, parallel reasoning, and large population work.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The orchestration around a bridge, choosing the context, holding the schema, reading results back, validating them, and deciding on any change, belongs to the controller or mission runner, never to the bridge itself.
public_glossary.example: The Bridge Phase Continuity Runtime is one concrete instance: the runtime unit that carries bounded bridge work across phases of a task and keeps a single dispatch-and-response round coherent over time.

example_route.gloss: open the runtime component that carries bridge work across phases
example_route.label: Bridge Phase Continuity Runtime

public_glossary.label: bridge
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Bridge means the repository's bounded external-worker transport. It is not a physical bridge, a generic software bridge, or an autonomous controller.
public_glossary.non_example: A bridge is not the system's conductor and not an autonomous agent that explores the codebase, runs many steps, or makes changes by itself. It is a one-packet-out, one-packet-back transport with all orchestration held outside it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A bridge is a one-round transport that sends a bounded context-and-instruction packet to an external worker and returns its response, without giving that worker independent browsing, iteration, or mutation control.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat anything a bridge returns as a worker's answer to a fixed packet, not as a decision the system has already acted on. The surrounding lane owns what was sent and what is done with the reply.

relationships.gloss: Bridge often powers observe/probe passes.
Kernel and controller surfaces launch and read bridge work.

public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the external worker lane and its dispatch and response machinery. A reader meets it wherever the site describes work sent to separate workers, such as parallel reasoning, research runs, or bulk population, and in the runtime component that carries this work across phases.
public_glossary.short_definition: A bridge is a one-round transport that sends a bounded context-and-instruction packet to an external worker and returns its response, without giving that worker independent browsing, iteration, or mutation control.

source_refs.gloss: Bridge runtime subsystem.
Bridge dispatch packet authoring.

public_glossary.card_definition: Building can compile code, render pages, package data, and validate invariants. A successful build proves that those configured transformations completed, not that every claim in the output is true.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Reproducible builds make the same declared inputs yield equivalent outputs, which turns unexplained drift into a diagnosable difference.
public_glossary.example: The public-site build turns the term registry into glossary cards and search records.
public_glossary.label: build
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Saving an edited source file is not the same as building its generated projections.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A build is the process, or the resulting artifact set, produced by transforming source files through declared tools and configuration.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Distinguish the build process from its outputs and record the source revision and toolchain used.
public_glossary.scope_note: A build covers the source inputs, configuration, tools, and outputs recorded for one invocation.
public_glossary.short_definition: A build is the process, or the resulting artifact set, produced by transforming source files through declared tools and configuration.

public_glossary.card_definition: A claim is easy to make and hard to check. The bundle is the checkable form: rather than describing what a component does, it ships the actual bodies, inputs, and outputs of a run in one place. That is the difference between reading an account of a check and holding the check. Bundles are metadata-only where the underlying data is private, so what you get is the shape and the verdict, not the substrate.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Bundles exist because this site publishes components whose full source is not published. Without them a reader would have to trust the summary. With them the trust moves to something narrower and testable: that the exported bytes match the source they claim to come from, which the build checks by digest on every run.
public_glossary.example: A component's exported bundle carries its source bodies under source_modules/, the fixtures it read, and the result record from the run, each digest-checked against live source.
public_glossary.label: bundle
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A bundle is a component's evidence packaged as files you can open: the source bodies it ran, the fixtures it read, and the result record it wrote, exported together so the run can be inspected without the private system.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a component claims something, open its bundle. If there is no bundle, you are reading a description rather than evidence.
public_glossary.scope_note: A bundle establishes what its own run covered. It is not a copy of the private system and does not stand in for one.
public_glossary.short_definition: A bundle is a component's evidence packaged as files you can open: the source bodies it ran, the fixtures it read, and the result record it wrote, exported together so the run can be inspected without the private system.

public_glossary.card_definition: Technical calls have inputs, a target, execution conditions, and an output or effect. In prose, called can also assign a name, so the surrounding grammar matters.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Issuing a call does not guarantee successful completion; errors, timeouts, refusal, or partial effects may follow.
public_glossary.example: The builder calls the link validator after generating the public pages.
public_glossary.label: call
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Mentioning a function's name is not the same as calling it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A call is an invocation that asks a function, command, service, tool, or person to perform a named operation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For an operational call, identify the invoked target, arguments, authority, and result.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers software invocations, tool requests, command execution, and explicit naming where context distinguishes them.
public_glossary.short_definition: A call is an invocation that asks a function, command, service, tool, or person to perform a named operation.

public_glossary.card_definition: Care is what turns a stake into upkeep. An agent acting with care makes maintenance, continuity, and the comprehension of whoever comes next into visible obligations: it fixes route gaps, preserves provenance, avoids bloating adapters, and leaves explicit closeout records of what was done. It is not a decorative value word. On this system it attaches to concrete actions such as running validators, probing routes, and recording receipts, so the care can be seen in evidence rather than merely asserted.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Care is one register within the broader judgment surface that governs how agents act on the system. It sits under the standards rather than floating free of them, so it can justify extra validation, clarity, and propagation work only when that work is anchored to evidence commands and recorded outcomes.
public_glossary.example: The Agent Completion Faithfulness Audit is care made concrete: it checks that a finished task left an accurate record of what was actually done, rather than a tidy claim the underlying files do not support.

example_route.gloss: open the audit that checks a finished task left an honest record
example_route.label: Agent Completion Faithfulness Audit

public_glossary.label: care
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Care is an operational judgment trait in the Type A register. The term does not claim emotion, consciousness, human virtue, or an external psychological classification.
public_glossary.non_example: Care is not sentiment, politeness, or a general value statement about doing good work. It is a specific obligation to leave upkeep behind: provenance, validation, and closeout records that the next agent can rely on.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Care is the judgment trait of treating correctness, human stakes, and future upkeep as part of the work, so a result is not merely produced but left findable, trustworthy, refreshable, and safe to extend.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When work here is described as done with care, look for the upkeep it left behind: a closeout record, a validator that ran, a preserved trail. Care that leaves no such trace is just a word.

relationships.gloss: Care is one trait supporting live controller judgment.
Care becomes practical through situated judgment and cheap truthful surfaces.
Care-driven local lessons should move to the owning plane when reusable.

public_glossary.scope_note: Care covers the maintenance-and-continuity dimension of how agents act on the system: protecting the next person or agent from re-deriving lost context, inheriting stale facts, or losing the original intent. A reader meets it across the agent reliability and continuity material, and in the audits that check whether a completed task left an honest, faithful record.
public_glossary.short_definition: Care is the judgment trait of treating correctness, human stakes, and future upkeep as part of the work, so a result is not merely produced but left findable, trustworthy, refreshable, and safe to extend.

source_refs.gloss: Codex-facing closeout and common-sense contract.
Claude-facing continuity and care posture.
Entry-surface compression rule that keeps care routeable rather than adapter-bloated.

public_glossary.card_definition: On this site, records carry fields, artifacts carry claims, and proof steps carry assumptions forward. The verb should identify what is conveyed and whether it remains unchanged.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Carrying a claim does not strengthen it; limitations and dependencies must travel with the claim if the transfer is faithful.
public_glossary.example: A public packet carries selected definitions from the registry into a downloadable artifact.
public_glossary.label: carry
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Repeating a claim without its evidence does not faithfully carry the original support.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To carry something is to contain, transport, preserve, or make it operative across a boundary or transition.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something carries information or authority, trace the source and the rule that permits the transfer.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers propagation of data, meaning, evidence, permissions, and assumptions.
public_glossary.short_definition: To carry something is to contain, transport, preserve, or make it operative across a boundary or transition.

public_glossary.card_definition: Dividing work into cases makes differences explicit: a rule may hold for one input class and fail for another. Covering several cases does not establish unexamined ones.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In proofs a case is a branch of an argument; in tests it is a concrete input and expected outcome; in both uses its boundary must be stated.
public_glossary.example: A proof may handle even and odd integers as two cases.
public_glossary.label: case
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: One successful case is not evidence that every possible case succeeds.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A case is one particular set of conditions or inputs considered separately inside a larger question, test, or proof.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check which conditions define the case and whether the collection of cases is complete.
public_glossary.scope_note: A case covers only the conditions, inputs, and branch named for it.
public_glossary.short_definition: A case is one particular set of conditions or inputs considered separately inside a larger question, test, or proof.

public_glossary.card_definition: Certificates are how a formal corpus grows to this size. Rather than proving each case by argument, a generator emits the data for each one and the proof checker confirms it. That is why declaration counts run to six figures while the number of distinct human ideas stays small: most of the corpus is checked, not written.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This is the exact gap between a very large verified corpus and a solved problem, and it is where the remaining work on these problems sits.
public_glossary.example: The corpus carries generated certificates for the finite cases, each checked by the Lean kernel.
public_glossary.label: certificate
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A certificate is a finite piece of data that makes a fact checkable by direct computation, so a machine can confirm the case rather than follow an argument.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A certificate establishes its own case. A family of them does not establish the general statement unless something proves the family covers it.
public_glossary.scope_note: A certificate covers the finite case it encodes.
public_glossary.short_definition: A certificate is a finite piece of data that makes a fact checkable by direct computation, so a machine can confirm the case rather than follow an argument.

public_glossary.card_definition: Changes should be described against a before-state and after-state. Their significance depends on the affected boundary, downstream consequences, and whether the transition was intended and authorized.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A visible file edit may be only one projection of a deeper source change, while a generated rewrite may alter many bytes without changing reader-visible meaning.
public_glossary.example: Adding a term changes the registry and, after rebuilding, the public glossary.
public_glossary.label: change
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Re-reading an unchanged file is an observation, not a change to the file.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A change is a transition by which something becomes different in content, state, location, behaviour, or interpretation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a change through its target, delta, reason, authority, and validation.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers durable and runtime transitions reported by the system.
public_glossary.short_definition: A change is a transition by which something becomes different in content, state, location, behaviour, or interpretation.

public_glossary.card_definition: A useful changelog tells readers what changed and often why, without reproducing every low-level edit. It supports orientation across versions but does not replace source history or validation evidence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Selection matters: a changelog is curated for readers, whereas a commit history records a finer-grained sequence of repository events.
public_glossary.example: A release note saying that glossary coverage increased is a changelog entry.
public_glossary.label: changelog
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A current feature list with no dates or change relationships is not a changelog.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A changelog is a chronological record of notable changes made to a project, product, document, or release.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a changelog to identify relevant changes, then inspect the linked source or release evidence for exact detail.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the public, reader-oriented history of significant updates.
public_glossary.short_definition: A changelog is a chronological record of notable changes made to a project, product, document, or release.

public_glossary.card_definition: Checks are the unit of evidence here. Each is a real command rather than a description of one, runs on your machine rather than a server, reads committed inputs, and leaves a result record behind. That is the whole mechanism: the claim says what should be true, the check finds out, and the record is what remains afterwards.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A check is only as informative as its ability to fail, which is why the negative cases matter more than the passing ones. A check that cannot fail is a formality with the appearance of rigour.
public_glossary.example: Each of the public components ships one check, its command written out in full.
public_glossary.label: check
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A check is a command you can run that tests one stated claim and writes down what it found.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Run the check. Reading about a check establishes nothing that running it would.
public_glossary.scope_note: A check establishes its own outcome on its own inputs, and nothing wider.
public_glossary.short_definition: A check is a command you can run that tests one stated claim and writes down what it found.

public_glossary.card_definition: Checkers make repeatable judgments over a bounded property such as syntax, links, types, or proof validity. Their result inherits both the strength and the blind spots of the encoded rules.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A checker can be fully correct about its own rule set while that rule set remains incomplete for a broader real-world goal.
public_glossary.example: The internal-link checker rejects a page whose href points to no generated target.
public_glossary.label: checker
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A human opinion without a stated evaluation rule is not an automated checker result.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A checker is a tool or procedure that evaluates an input against explicit rules and reports whether those rules are satisfied.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a checker result together with the rules it implements, the inputs it examined, and its failure behaviour.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers automated and procedural validation tools shown in the site's evidence chain.
public_glossary.short_definition: A checker is a tool or procedure that evaluates an input against explicit rules and reports whether those rules are satisfied.

public_glossary.card_definition: Every component here states its claim in one place and ships its check in another. Keeping them apart is what makes the pair checkable: a claim that drifts wider than its evidence becomes visible as a mismatch rather than blending into the surrounding description. The wording of a claim is treated as an artefact in its own right, and edits to it are checked.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The failure this guards against is gradual. Nobody rewrites a claim into a lie; wording widens a little at a time until it covers ground the evidence never did, which is why the relationship is registered rather than remembered.
public_glossary.example: A component states one claim and includes one check; the release gate refuses wording that reaches past what the check ran.
public_glossary.label: claim
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A claim is a stated assertion about what something does or establishes, written down separately from the evidence for it so the two can be compared.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the claim and the check together. A claim with no check behind it is a description.
public_glossary.scope_note: A claim establishes nothing by itself. Its evidence does, and only as far as the evidence reaches.
public_glossary.short_definition: A claim is a stated assertion about what something does or establishes, written down separately from the evidence for it so the two can be compared.

public_glossary.card_definition: A proof corpus does not say what it means. The registry is where each public assertion is written down with its status, which formal statement supports it, and how far it reaches. Keeping it separate is what allows a check that the wording still matches the mathematics after either changes.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Most of the corpus is deliberately not registered: checking a declaration does not promote it into a reviewed public claim, and treating those as the same thing would let unreviewed work inherit reviewed standing.
public_glossary.example: The registry records 101 claims by status, alongside statements explicitly recorded as not claimed.
public_glossary.label: claim registry
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Here, the claim registry is the reviewed map from public mathematical claims to their status, formal support, and open boundary; it is not an inventory of every Lean declaration.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The claim registry is the reviewed list of what the formal work is asserted to establish, kept separately from the proofs themselves.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The registry states the claims. The corpus states the theorems. Compare them.
public_glossary.scope_note: The registry covers the claims recorded in it, not everything the corpus contains.
public_glossary.short_definition: The claim registry is the reviewed list of what the formal work is asserted to establish, kept separately from the proofs themselves.

source_refs.gloss: Grounds this Plectis-specific definition and its scope.

public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis uses class in two explicit senses: a semantic or status class groups rows under one governed rule, while a software class defines instances and behaviour. The field or surrounding code must choose the sense; a label such as evidence class does not imply Python inheritance.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Class membership is deliberately only one axis. An agent class, evidence class, or failure class does not silently confer authority, quality, status, or permission unless the governing contract says so.
public_glossary.example: A validator can place each finding into a failure class with a specific repair route.
public_glossary.label: class
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Calling two items similar without a membership rule does not define a class.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A class is a category of things treated as sharing selected properties or, in programming, a definition for a family of objects and behaviour.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Resolve class from the owning schema or code locus, then ask which properties membership guarantees and which other axes remain independent.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers typed categories in audits, evidence, failures, and software descriptions.
public_glossary.short_definition: A class is a category of things treated as sharing selected properties or, in programming, a definition for a family of objects and behaviour.

public_glossary.card_definition: The relevant check must be named: a clean worktree has no reported file changes, while a clean validation has no detected violations. Cleanliness is therefore bounded by the detector and target.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A clean result does not prove the absence of defects that the check was not designed or able to detect.
public_glossary.example: A scoped Git status is clean when it reports no modifications for the named files.
public_glossary.label: clean
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A quiet command output is not proof of cleanliness unless silence is its documented success signal.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Clean describes a condition with no detected unwanted residue, conflict, error, or modification under a stated check.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read clean as shorthand for a specific observed condition and find the command or rule that established it.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers repository state, generated output, validation, data, and operational cleanup.
public_glossary.short_definition: Clean describes a condition with no detected unwanted residue, conflict, error, or modification under a stated check.

public_glossary.card_definition: Cloning is the first step in every route on this site that produces evidence rather than description. It needs no account and no permission, which is deliberate: the checks are meant to be run by people with no relationship to the author.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A clone is a copy at a moment in time. It goes stale as the published repository moves, which is why a result from an old local copy can describe a version nobody else can obtain.
public_glossary.example: The quickstart begins by cloning the repository, then runs the first check against it.
public_glossary.label: clone
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To clone a repository is to copy it, with its full history, onto your own machine so you can run and inspect it locally.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Cloning is how you stop taking this site's word for anything.
public_glossary.scope_note: A clone reflects the repository at the moment it was copied.
public_glossary.short_definition: To clone a repository is to copy it, with its full history, onto your own machine so you can run and inspect it locally.

public_glossary.card_definition: Closing a task, question, claim, or route requires different evidence. The word should name the condition that changed and any residual work deliberately left outside the closure.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A closed loop records the result and connects it back to the surface that requested or governs the work.
public_glossary.example: A task closes when its requested change is landed, validated, and recorded under the governing process.
public_glossary.label: close
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Stopping work because time ran out does not by itself close the task.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To close something is to complete its required ending conditions or make it no longer open for further action in its current state.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat closure as scoped: verify exactly what is closed and which conditions establish it.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers bounded completion states, not physical closure.
public_glossary.short_definition: To close something is to complete its required ending conditions or make it no longer open for further action in its current state.

public_glossary.card_definition: Work that ends without a closeout leaves the next reader to reconstruct it. The closeout records the landed change, the residue, and the boundary of what was attempted, so a session can be picked up without archaeology. It also names what was left alone on purpose, which is otherwise indistinguishable from what was forgotten.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The hardest thing to record honestly is the deliberate omission, because it reads like a gap. Naming it is what separates a bounded piece of work from an unfinished one.
public_glossary.example: A closeout that reports a landed commit, a clean owned slice, and a list of paths left to their own owner is complete; one that reports only the commit is not.
public_glossary.label: closeout
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Closeout is the recorded landing of one bounded unit of work—change, validation, residue, deliberate omissions, and handoff—not merely the final chat message or the fact that editing stopped.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Closeout is the end of a unit of work: the point at which what changed, what is still open, and what was deliberately not done are recorded, before the work is handed on.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a closeout for what it says was not done. That is usually the part that matters.
public_glossary.scope_note: A closeout describes one unit of work. It makes no claim about the surrounding system.
public_glossary.short_definition: Closeout is the end of a unit of work: the point at which what changed, what is still open, and what was deliberately not done are recorded, before the work is handed on.

Grounds this Plectis-specific definition and its scope.

public_glossary.card_definition: Code may implement a program, specify data transformations, or state formal proofs. Its presence does not show that it has been run, tested, or reviewed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Source code is a readable input; generated code, compiled binaries, and runtime behavior are distinct artifacts connected by a toolchain.
public_glossary.example: The Lean source states the formal theorem that the proof checker verifies.
public_glossary.label: code
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Pseudocode or prose describing a procedure is not executable code unless a tool accepts it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Code is text written in a programming or formal language so a computer or proof checker can parse and act on it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Inspect the language, version, dependencies, and execution evidence before making claims from code.
public_glossary.scope_note: Code covers the text and language version in the named file or module.
public_glossary.short_definition: Code is text written in a programming or formal language so a computer or proof checker can parse and act on it.

public_glossary.card_definition: Coding turns an intended operation into source that a machine or checker can interpret. It includes design choices and validation, not only typing characters.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Code can be syntactically valid yet fail its purpose, so implementation intent and observable behaviour remain part of the work.
public_glossary.example: Adding a deterministic glossary builder rule is coding.
public_glossary.label: coding
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Pasting generated text without understanding or validating its effect is not complete coding work.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Coding is the activity of expressing instructions, data structures, and behaviour in a programming or formal language.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Judge coding work by the behaviour and constraints of the resulting source, together with focused checks.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers authoring and revising software and formal proof source.
public_glossary.short_definition: Coding is the activity of expressing instructions, data structures, and behaviour in a programming or formal language.

public_glossary.card_definition: The distinction decides what a review can establish. A coding agent clones the repository and runs the checks, so its report rests on runs that happened. A browser assistant reads the same pages and cites them, which is useful orientation but establishes nothing about whether the code works. This site separates the two routes deliberately rather than letting a reader assume any AI review is equivalent.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The asymmetry is not about model quality. A capable assistant that cannot execute is still limited to restating what the repository says about itself, which is exactly the claim under test.
public_glossary.example: The setup prompt on the landing page is written for a coding agent: it clones both repositories and runs the first checks, then reports exit codes.
public_glossary.label: coding agent
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A coding agent is an AI tool that can run commands on your machine, such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, as distinguished from a chat assistant that can only read and quote.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask which route produced a review. What an agent ran is evidence; what it summarised is not.
public_glossary.scope_note: A coding agent establishes what it actually ran on your machine. It does not establish anything it only read.
public_glossary.short_definition: A coding agent is an AI tool that can run commands on your machine, such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, as distinguished from a chat assistant that can only read and quote.

public_glossary.card_definition: A cold agent is a coding or reasoning agent that opens this system fresh, without the context a previous session would have carried, and without any unwritten shared knowledge to fall back on. To act safely it has to read the source, the standards, and the recorded state, and from those work out what each thing does, what opens it, what proves it, and what comes next. The system is designed so that this is possible: orientation comes from the artifacts, not from folklore held in someone's head.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The cold-agent frame is a deliberate test the system applies to itself: every artifact should name what it does, what opens it, what proves it, and what comes next, so that an agent with no memory can make the next safe decision without re-deriving the whole system. It is the discipline that lets work continue across a wiped session, a switch of machine, or a handover between people and agents.
public_glossary.example: The "With a coding agent" page is a concrete instance: it walks a coding agent that has just been pointed at the system through its first moves, assuming no earlier context, which is exactly the cold-agent situation.

example_route.gloss: see the first moves a fresh agent is walked through
example_route.label: With a coding agent

public_glossary.label: cold agent
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A cold agent is a capable agent with no prior-session memory that must orient from durable artifacts; cold describes context, not intelligence, experience, or tool access.
public_glossary.non_example: A cold agent is not a less capable or restricted agent, and not a person new to the team. It is a fully capable agent that simply begins with no session memory and must orient from the written artifacts rather than from remembered context.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A cold agent is a capable software agent beginning with no conversation history or memory of earlier work, forced to orient entirely from the durable files and routes available on disk.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a page assumes a cold agent, it is assuming you arrive with no prior context and everything you need is on the page or one click away. Take it at face value: if something cannot be worked out from the written artifacts, that is a gap in the system, not knowledge you were expected to already have.

relationships.gloss: Cold agents orient through affordance rows, not file crawls.
Cold boot begins at the navigation seed.
Cold agent is the unprimed-session shape of a Type A controller.

public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the kind of agent the documentation, standards, and entry surfaces are written for: one with no prior-session memory. A reader meets it across the entry and orientation pages, the coding-agent guide, and the Cold-Reader Route Map, wherever the system explains how a fresh agent is meant to find its way in.
public_glossary.short_definition: A cold agent is a capable software agent beginning with no conversation history or memory of earlier work, forced to orient entirely from the durable files and routes available on disk.

source_refs.gloss: Cold-agent self-comprehension north star.
Cold-boot navigation ladder.
CLAUDE.md opens with cold-agent bootstrap discipline.

public_glossary.card_definition: Software usually works on the machine that built it. A cold clone removes that advantage: nothing is cached, no local configuration is present, and no undeclared dependency is quietly satisfied. It is the cheapest way to find out whether what was published is what was tested, and it routinely finds gaps that pass on the author's laptop.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This matters more here than usual, because local checkouts of a published repository drift quickly. A result taken from a stale working copy can describe a version nobody else can obtain, which is a claim about the author's disk rather than about the release.
public_glossary.example: The cold-clone probe runs on a fresh clone of a tagged release and writes its result to .microcosm/cold_clone_probe.json.
public_glossary.label: cold clone
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A cold clone is a clean checkout used to test the published repository without the author’s caches or local configuration; it is not just any Git clone or a proof of all-environment correctness.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A cold clone is a fresh copy of a repository on a machine that has never seen it, used to check that the published thing works for a stranger rather than only for its author.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a cold-clone result as evidence that the named published revision and declared commands work without the author’s local state; do not extend it to environments or behaviors the probe did not exercise.
public_glossary.scope_note: A cold-clone probe establishes only how the named revision, environment, and commands behaved in that run. It does not prove every supported environment or the correctness of the release as a whole.
public_glossary.short_definition: A cold clone is a fresh copy of a repository on a machine that has never seen it, used to check that the published thing works for a stranger rather than only for its author.

public_glossary.card_definition: Combinatorial questions often ask how many configurations exist or whether a particular arrangement must occur. Proofs use counting, extremal arguments, probability, algebra, and graph structure.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Many problems associated with Erdős connect combinatorics with number theory, probability, and discrete geometry.
public_glossary.example: A graph-colouring problem is combinatorial because it studies discrete assignments under adjacency constraints.
public_glossary.label: combinatorics
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A purely numerical calculation is not combinatorics unless it represents a discrete structural question.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Combinatorics is the area of mathematics that studies finite or discrete arrangements, selections, counts, and structural patterns.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the objects being arranged or counted and which configurations are considered distinct.
public_glossary.scope_note: Combinatorics covers the discrete objects, constraints, and counting or existence questions in the stated problem.
public_glossary.short_definition: Combinatorics is the area of mathematics that studies finite or discrete arrangements, selections, counts, and structural patterns.

public_glossary.card_definition: A command names the program and arguments to run, but its effect also depends on the working directory, environment, permissions, and input files. Displaying a command is not evidence that it was executed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Commands can read, create, change, publish, or delete state, so their authority and risk come from the invoked operation rather than the text alone.
public_glossary.example: A check command can rebuild the site and compare every generated file with disk.
public_glossary.label: command
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A copied command with no execution receipt is not a test result.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A command is a concrete instruction submitted to a program, shell, or tool through its command interface.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Record the command with its environment and result when reproducibility matters.
public_glossary.scope_note: A command covers one invocation with its stated arguments and execution context.
public_glossary.short_definition: A command is a concrete instruction submitted to a program, shell, or tool through its command interface.

public_glossary.card_definition: Commits are what make a history checkable rather than assertable. Each has a hash that identifies its exact contents, so citing a commit pins a claim to a specific state of the files rather than to whatever they say today. When something here reports a commit hash, that is the receipt.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A hash is not a signature. It proves which bytes, not who wrote them or whether they are correct.
public_glossary.example: A deploy receipt cites the commit it published, so the live site can be traced to exact source.
public_glossary.label: commit
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A commit is one recorded change to a repository, carrying its own identifier, author, timestamp and complete contents.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When work is reported as done, look for the commit. The hash names exactly what changed.
public_glossary.scope_note: A commit establishes what changed and when. It says nothing about whether the change was right.
public_glossary.short_definition: A commit is one recorded change to a repository, carrying its own identifier, author, timestamp and complete contents.

public_glossary.card_definition: In this system common sense is the live judgment that connects fixed governance to the case in front of an agent. It reads the axioms, standards, routes, and recorded state, applies ordinary intelligence to the specific situation, checks whether the names and routes it assumes actually resolve, and acts on the cheapest truthful surface available. When the work reveals a reusable gap, such as a missing route, standard, or recorded fact, the lesson is folded back into the artifact that owns it, with the originating case cited. It is the non-brittle part of the system's intelligence: source-backed and testable rather than improvised.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Its defining discipline is that the judgment must stay reusable: routes are expected to resolve through the system's own lookups, facts that can change are projected or queried rather than frozen, and a durable local lesson is propagated up into the owning artifact so a later agent can rely on it.
public_glossary.example: The area page on agent reliability and safety is a concrete home for this term: it gathers the components that govern how an agent infers a correct, source-backed action and records what it learned, which is common sense in operation.

example_route.gloss: see where situated agent judgment lives on the site
example_route.label: Area: agent reliability & safety

public_glossary.label: common sense
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Common sense is a local instruction to exercise bounded judgment and propagate reusable lessons; it is not claimed as a universal faculty or scientific construct.
public_glossary.non_example: Common sense is not ungoverned instinct, intuition, or a licence to improvise outside the rules. It is judgment bound to the system's axioms, standards, and live state, and incomplete until any reusable lesson is propagated back.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Common sense is governed, situation-aware judgment that combines the current state and surrounding rules to infer the right bounded action when no bespoke instruction spells it out.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a result is described as reached by common sense, read it as a judgment derived from the system's stated rules and live state, not as a guess. It should be traceable back to the routes, facts, and standards it drew on.

relationships.gloss: Common sense is one Type A judgment trait.
The controller is responsible for applying situated judgment.
Reusable common-sense lessons move upward into shared artifacts.
The axiom-candidate lane decides whether common sense becomes constitutional.

public_glossary.scope_note: Common sense covers how agents move from the system's explicit governance to a correct action on a particular task, and how they feed reusable lessons back into shared surfaces. A reader meets it across the agent reliability and continuity areas of the site, wherever judgment, repair, and lesson propagation are described.
public_glossary.short_definition: Common sense is governed, situation-aware judgment that combines the current state and surrounding rules to infer the right bounded action when no bespoke instruction spells it out.

source_refs.gloss: The closeout move that turns local common sense into durable shared grammar.
Compressed entry-surface doctrine for cold-agent visibility.

public_glossary.card_definition: A compact view omits lower-priority detail so a reader can scan or choose quickly. It should retain routes to fuller evidence and make its omissions or boundary understandable.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Good compression preserves decision-relevant distinctions; merely making text shorter can erase the very boundary a reader needs.
public_glossary.example: A compact term card gives the definition and scope while linking to deeper material.
public_glossary.label: compact
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Truncated text that removes the qualification from a claim is not a faithful compact view.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Compact describes material reduced in size or detail while preserving the information needed for its intended use.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat compact material as a navigation or decision aid and open the deeper source when omitted detail matters.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers condensed cards, summaries, packets, and interface layouts.
public_glossary.short_definition: Compact describes material reduced in size or detail while preserving the information needed for its intended use.

public_glossary.card_definition: When a site is renamed or reorganised, links and identifiers that people already hold would otherwise break. A compatibility route is the machinery that keeps those old paths resolving: a tombstone page, a redirect, an alias, or a manifest entry that takes the visitor to the current location. It names the old route, the new route, the behaviour, and the scope, so the move is visible rather than silent.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A compatibility route is public migration infrastructure: it prevents broken links and keeps the history of earlier addresses inspectable, while making the current identity, Plectis, unmistakable. It does not rewrite the past or imply that the old name is endorsed.
public_glossary.example: The old Microcosm site root is a compatibility route: it shows a tombstone and forwards visitors to the current Plectis site rather than serving the former content as if it were still live.

example_route.gloss: open the component that maps readers from any entry point to the current surface
example_route.label: Cold Reader Route Map

public_glossary.label: compatibility route
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A compatibility route preserves a retired URL or identifier by forwarding it to the current Plectis object; it is not a second live identity or an endorsement of the retired name.
public_glossary.non_example: A compatibility route is not evidence that the old name is still the current brand, and it is not a separate active site running in parallel. It is a one-way bridge from a retired address to the live one.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A compatibility route is an old URL or identifier retained solely to redirect readers to the current Plectis surface, preserving access without reviving the retired name as the live one.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a compatibility route as a forwarding link, not as a second live site. Where it leads is the current surface; the old address it came from is retired.

relationships.gloss: Microcosm is now a legacy/compatibility label.
Compatibility routes point to the current public identity.
Compatibility behavior is a routing concern.

public_glossary.scope_note: Covers retired Microcosm-era URLs, source paths, and identifiers that must continue resolving after the move to Plectis. A reader meets one whenever an old link or bookmark lands on a tombstone or redirect that points to the current page.
public_glossary.short_definition: A compatibility route is an old URL or identifier retained solely to redirect readers to the current Plectis surface, preserving access without reviving the retired name as the live one.
