Legacy site root tombstone for old Microcosm URLs.

public_glossary.card_definition: In this system compression is governed, not casual. Every compact summary is produced under a declared profile that fixes how much detail a given band carries, so a one-line entry, a card, and a full module are different rungs of the same material rather than arbitrary trims. Each row records what was preserved and what was omitted, and keeps a path back to the source it stands for, so a reader can always open the fuller layer beneath any summary.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Compression here is the write side of navigation: standards declare the readable shapes, profiles declare the band contracts, and the resulting summaries are generated surfaces that let later readers spend attention deliberately. Where no profile governs a row, the system records a profile gap instead of inventing an ad hoc summary.
public_glossary.example: The Navigation Hologram Route Plane is a concrete instance: it is the running surface that holds these banded, profile-governed views and the routes that let a reader move from a compact row down to its source.

example_route.gloss: open the component that turns source material into banded, drillable views
example_route.label: Navigation Hologram Route Plane

public_glossary.label: compression
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Compression means preservation of meaning across governed navigation bands. It is not data compression, model compression, or summarization in every external use.
public_glossary.non_example: Compression is not minification, lossy file shrinking, or a loose vibe summary. It is preservation through declared bands that always names its omissions and keeps a route back to the original material.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Compression is the governed reduction of larger source material into a smaller navigable view that records what it preserves, what it omits, which profile and band shaped it, and how to reopen the authoritative source.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a compressed row as a faithful but partial view: it carries an omission record and a route back to source, so when detail matters, follow that route rather than relying on the short form alone.

relationships.gloss: Profiles own legal compression contracts.
Bands are the compression packet levels.
Compression creates rows navigation can traverse.
Worker compression should be bounded as a row job.
Standards declare what must remain readable.

public_glossary.scope_note: Compression governs how the public pages, component cards, paper modules, and field-guide entries are derived from the underlying files and records. A reader meets it wherever a short summary stands in for a larger artifact and offers a way to open the fuller layer.
public_glossary.short_definition: Compression is the governed reduction of larger source material into a smaller navigable view that records what it preserves, what it omits, which profile and band shaped it, and how to reopen the authoritative source.

source_refs.gloss: General compression skill for non-raw-seed rows.
Compression-as-navigation theory roof.

public_glossary.card_definition: Each profile is tied to a specific artifact kind, such as a voice record, a relational map, a peer-knowledge note, or a term definition. It names the bands the artifact can be projected into, the schema each band must follow, the evidence policy, and the validation check, so that a cheap automated worker, a larger model, and a person all shorten the same artifact into the same shape. Four profiles run today, covering voice records, relational maps, peer-knowledge notes, and vocabulary terms.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Profiles are registered together so that compression behaves as a governed primitive: the stated design target is that every artifact kind eventually names its own profile, so that any worker producing a band yields an identical row shape.
public_glossary.example: The vocabulary-term profile is a concrete compression profile: it governs how a vocabulary term is projected into a word, a phrase, a flag, a card, and deeper bands, which is the same laddered shape this glossary entry follows.

example_route.label: Navigation Hologram Route Plane

public_glossary.label: compression profile
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A compression profile governs the depth bands and allowed omissions for one artifact kind; it is not a file-compression setting or an improvised summary style.
public_glossary.non_example: A compression profile is not a file-size or data-compression setting, and not a one-off summary someone writes by hand. It is a declared rulebook, bound to a specific artifact kind, stating which details a shortened form must keep and which collapses are not allowed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A compression profile is the repeatable rulebook for shortening one artifact kind, specifying its depth bands, mandatory content, allowed omissions, and forbidden collapses.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a piece of content here is shown at varying lengths, the compression profile is what fixed which details had to survive and which were allowed to fall away; read it to know what a short form is guaranteed to still carry.

relationships.gloss: Each profile declares its legal bands and contracts.
Rows are emitted under a profile.
Profiles are schema-grade contracts.

public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the rulebooks that govern banded compression across the system. A reader meets it behind any surface that presents the same content at different levels of detail, and it is grounded in the navigation and route-plane machinery that projects artifacts through bands.
public_glossary.short_definition: A compression profile is the repeatable rulebook for shortening one artifact kind, specifying its depth bands, mandatory content, allowed omissions, and forbidden collapses.

public_glossary.card_definition: Concepts are the system's defined nouns, as distinct from its procedures. Each one fixes a single object or idea, gives it a stable identifier and a short description, links to where it is defined in the source, and connects to the mechanisms and principles that use it. Together they form the shared ontology that mechanisms act on and principles reason about, so that a recurring object keeps one settled meaning across the whole system.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A concept is curated and source-linked rather than improvised, which is how the system keeps its vocabulary from drifting as it grows. It names a thing; the steps that act on that thing live in mechanisms and skills, not in the concept itself.
public_glossary.example: Executable Doctrine Grammar is one such named object: a defined idea in the system's doctrine that fixes what it means for a rule to be runnable before it is treated as authoritative, carrying a stable name other doctrine can refer to.

example_route.gloss: open one named doctrine object and read what it fixes
example_route.label: Executable Doctrine Grammar

public_glossary.label: concept
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Concept means a governed doctrine entity with a stable id and sources. It does not mean every idea or assert that the local definition is philosophically exhaustive.
public_glossary.non_example: A concept is not a step, a procedure, or a tool you run. It is the name and definition of an object, not the action taken on it; the doing belongs to mechanisms and skills.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A concept is a curated vocabulary entry that gives a recurring object, abstraction, or class of meaning one stable identifier and definition for other system records to reference consistently.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a concept as the settled meaning of one named object. When something else on the site refers to it, read the concept to learn exactly what that object is, not how to do anything with it.

relationships.gloss: Concepts are doctrine nodes.
Concepts name objects; mechanisms name movement.

public_glossary.scope_note: Concepts cover the named objects in the doctrine layer, distinct from anti-patterns, axioms, and principles. A reader meets them wherever the doctrine refers to a defined object by name, and on the doctrine pages where those objects are listed and described.
public_glossary.short_definition: A concept is a curated vocabulary entry that gives a recurring object, abstraction, or class of meaning one stable identifier and definition for other system records to reference consistently.

Concept/mechanism curation workflow.

public_glossary.card_definition: Reductions are real work and are routinely mistaken for progress towards a solution. What a reduction establishes is that the target now rests on a named, unproved hypothesis; whether that is easier than the original is a separate judgement nobody has made. The registry records these separately from unconditional results for that reason.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The honest accounting is that a reduction moves the difficulty and reports where it went. Counting reductions alongside proofs would make a portfolio of open problems look like a portfolio of results.
public_glossary.example: 39 of the 100 registered claims are conditional reductions, held separately from the 37 proved outright.
public_glossary.label: conditional reduction
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A conditional reduction proves that one statement would follow from another that is not itself proved, converting a problem into a different problem rather than solving it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For a conditional result, find the hypothesis it rests on. Nothing is settled until that is proved.
public_glossary.scope_note: A conditional reduction establishes an implication, not its conclusion.
public_glossary.short_definition: A conditional reduction proves that one statement would follow from another that is not itself proved, converting a problem into a different problem rather than solving it.

public_glossary.card_definition: Confirmation reduces uncertainty by checking a proposition through an appropriate observation or independent route. Its strength depends on whether the new evidence is genuinely informative rather than a repeat of the same unverified source.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Confirmation supports a claim within the check's boundary but does not eliminate untested alternatives or future change.
public_glossary.example: A registry audit confirms that all requested term ids are present and unique.
public_glossary.label: confirm
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Rephrasing the original claim does not independently confirm it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To confirm something is to obtain additional evidence that supports an existing expectation, claim, identity, or result.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a check confirms a claim, identify the proposition tested and whether the evidence is independent or merely derivative.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers verification of state, identity, output, links, and research claims.
public_glossary.short_definition: To confirm something is to obtain additional evidence that supports an existing expectation, claim, identity, or result.

public_glossary.card_definition: Conjectures are informed research targets, often supported by examples, computation, analogy, or partial theorems. Those supports do not change the conjecture's unproved status.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A conjecture may be reformulated into equivalent statements or divided into cases without becoming solved, and a catalogue can update its status as the literature changes.
public_glossary.example: An Erdős problem can ask whether a stated property always holds, making that proposed universal statement a conjecture.
public_glossary.label: conjecture
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A theorem is not a conjecture once its proof has been accepted under the stated assumptions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A conjecture is a precise mathematical statement believed or suspected to be true but not yet proved or disproved.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a conjecture as an open claim until a valid proof or counterexample settles it.
public_glossary.scope_note: A conjecture covers the exact statement and hypotheses in its cited formulation.
public_glossary.short_definition: A conjecture is a precise mathematical statement believed or suspected to be true but not yet proved or disproved.

public_glossary.card_definition: Connections make the site usable as a map rather than a pile of pages. A useful connection says not only where the other item is but why it is relevant—for example, that one file generated another or that one result supports a claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A connection may be a hyperlink, source reference, typed relation, dependency edge, or command route; its meaning comes from the recorded relation, not from adjacency alone.
public_glossary.example: A glossary card connects a term to the component page where the term is used in a real example.
public_glossary.label: connect
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Items listed on the same page are not necessarily connected in any semantic or evidential sense.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To connect two items is to give a reader or program a traversable route from one to the other, usually with a label explaining their relationship.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Follow the relationship label as well as the link, because a connection does not by itself mean equivalence, support, or authority.
public_glossary.scope_note: A connection covers the declared route and relationship between two named items.
public_glossary.short_definition: To connect two items is to give a reader or program a traversable route from one to the other, usually with a label explaining their relationship.

public_glossary.card_definition: A contact point may be an email address, form, profile, or named route. Publishing it says how communication can begin, not that every message will receive a reply or produce an agreement.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Reachability, consent, identity, and responsiveness are separate properties even when one contact address is public.
public_glossary.example: A public email link is a contact point for a reader with a relevant question.
public_glossary.label: contact
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Mentioning someone's name without a supported route does not create permission to contact them anywhere.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Contact is a supported way to reach a person, team, or service or the act of doing so.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use the contact method for the purpose it states and respect its audience and privacy boundary.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the communication route explicitly offered by the site.
public_glossary.short_definition: Contact is a supported way to reach a person, team, or service or the act of doing so.

public_glossary.card_definition: Content can be prose, data, code, diagrams, or structured records. Its format and location do not by themselves determine its authority.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The same underlying content can be projected into several formats, so identity and source pointers matter when deciding whether two surfaces are copies or independent claims.
public_glossary.example: The glossary card's content includes its definition, scope, example, and non-example.
public_glossary.label: content
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A file path or access permission is not the content stored at that location.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Content is the human- or machine-readable material carried by an artifact, apart from the container, route, and permissions around it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separate what an artifact contains from what the artifact is allowed to establish.
public_glossary.scope_note: Content covers the material present in the named artifact and version.
public_glossary.short_definition: Content is the human- or machine-readable material carried by an artifact, apart from the container, route, and permissions around it.

public_glossary.card_definition: The same word, result, or action can mean different things under different goals, files, environments, or prior statements. Context supplies those constraints without necessarily becoming part of the thing itself.
public_glossary.deep_definition: More context is not automatically better; useful context is selected for the decision while preserving the boundaries that prevent misinterpretation.
public_glossary.example: The word pass needs context to distinguish a validation result from one traversal of a process.
public_glossary.label: context
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: An isolated sentence copied away from its qualification lacks the context needed for the original claim.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Context is the surrounding information, conditions, and relationships needed to interpret something appropriately.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Before interpreting a term or result, identify the relevant audience, task, source, time, and surrounding claims.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers semantic, operational, historical, and task-specific surroundings named by the site.
public_glossary.short_definition: Context is the surrounding information, conditions, and relationships needed to interpret something appropriately.

public_glossary.card_definition: AI sessions end, contexts fill, and machines restart. Continuity is the discipline of writing enough to disk that the next actor can pick up safely rather than guessing, and of being explicit about what is unfinished. It is one of the seven areas the components are grouped into.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The failure is subtle: a handoff that reads confidently but omits what was uncertain leaves the next actor repeating settled work or trusting an unchecked claim.
public_glossary.example: Work continuity is one of the seven areas on the architecture map.
public_glossary.label: continuity
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Continuity is the problem of carrying work across a break, so that a session which stops mid-task can be resumed without reconstructing what was happening.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Continuity work is judged by whether a stranger could resume from what was written down.
public_glossary.scope_note: Continuity components establish behaviour on their own recorded scenarios.
public_glossary.short_definition: Continuity is the problem of carrying work across a break, so that a session which stops mid-task can be resumed without reconstructing what was happening.

public_glossary.card_definition: In a proof by contradiction, the target is established by assuming its opposite and showing that assumption forces an impossibility. The proof is only as strong as the chain from the assumption to the contradiction.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Irrationality proofs commonly assume a series is rational, extract a finite denominator or repeating pattern, and then show the required arithmetic structure cannot exist.
public_glossary.example: Assuming a sum is rational may force an integer strictly between zero and one, yielding a contradiction.
public_glossary.label: contradiction
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Two surprising or tension-filled statements are not a contradiction unless they cannot both be true.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A contradiction is an impossible conclusion—such as a statement and its negation both holding—derived from a set of assumptions.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the assumption being rejected and the exact impossible statement it produces.
public_glossary.scope_note: A contradiction rejects the assumptions used to derive it within the logic and hypotheses of that proof.
public_glossary.short_definition: A contradiction is an impossible conclusion—such as a statement and its negation both holding—derived from a set of assumptions.

public_glossary.card_definition: Control may be exercised by a rule, interface, permission boundary, feedback loop, or person. It differs from observation because it can affect what happens rather than merely report it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Good control has a bounded target and visible feedback; otherwise direction can be applied without knowing whether it had the intended effect.
public_glossary.example: A release gate controls whether generated files may be published.
public_glossary.label: control
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A dashboard that only displays status does not control the underlying process.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Control is the ability or mechanism used to direct behaviour, constrain choices, or authorize changes.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a surface is called control, identify which decisions it can make and which state it is permitted to change.
public_glossary.scope_note: Here the term covers operational direction and authorization within the system's stated boundaries.
public_glossary.short_definition: Control is the ability or mechanism used to direct behaviour, constrain choices, or authorize changes.

public_glossary.card_definition: A convergent series has a well-defined sum even though no finite stage contains every term. Convergence says that the value exists; it does not say whether that value is rational, algebraic, transcendental, or easy to compute.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Proofs control the tail left after a partial sum to show that all later sums remain arbitrarily close to one value, replacing an informal picture of settling down with a quantified statement.
public_glossary.example: A reciprocal series may converge because its denominators grow fast enough, while its sum's irrationality remains open.
public_glossary.label: convergence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Terms tending to zero are necessary but not sufficient for a series to converge.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Convergence means the partial sums of an infinite series approach one fixed finite value as more terms are included.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separate the question of whether a series converges from the question of what kind of number its limit is.
public_glossary.scope_note: Convergence applies to one sequence or series under the stated ordering and notion of distance.
public_glossary.short_definition: Convergence means the partial sums of an infinite series approach one fixed finite value as more terms are included.

public_glossary.card_definition: Coprime does not require either number to be prime; 8 and 15 are coprime even though both are composite. The condition is what lets modular inverses and multiplicative orders exist.
public_glossary.deep_definition: When a base is coprime to a denominator, repeated multiplication by that base cycles among invertible residue classes rather than collapsing to zero.
public_glossary.example: A finite denominator certificate checks that the base is coprime to the reduced denominator.
public_glossary.label: coprime
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Two numbers can share no obvious small factor and still fail to be coprime.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Two integers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is one, meaning they share no prime factor.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check coprimality with respect to the exact pair of integers named in the result.
public_glossary.scope_note: Coprime is a relation between the stated integers or sets of integers.
public_glossary.short_definition: Two integers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is one, meaning they share no prime factor.

public_glossary.card_definition: A copy may preserve the source exactly or transform it during copying. Its usefulness depends on knowing what it copies, when it was made, and whether later source changes are expected to propagate.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Exactness is a claim about correspondence at a particular time, while freshness asks whether the source has changed since then.
public_glossary.example: A generated public page is a readable copy of selected registry content.
public_glossary.label: copy
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A paraphrase is not an exact copy even when it conveys a similar idea.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A copy is a reproduction of material placed in another location or representation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a copy as secondary material unless an explicit rule promotes it to authority.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers duplicated files, projected prose, and copied data within the named source relationship.
public_glossary.short_definition: A copy is a reproduction of material placed in another location or representation.

public_glossary.card_definition: In Plectis, corpus means an enumerated body against which a count, proof, or check is made: for example, the published PDFs, Lean declarations, or another manifest-backed collection. Fixing membership makes the claim reproducible; a result over one corpus does not extend to future files or excluded material.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Corpus is a measurement boundary, not a claim of representativeness or completeness. Plectis reports both raw declaration counts and deduplicated statement counts because the same fixed corpus can support different legitimate units.
public_glossary.example: The papers corpus is the fixed set of published PDFs the release chain checks.
public_glossary.label: corpus
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A corpus is a fixed body of material treated as one collection, so results can be quoted against a known set rather than an open-ended one.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Locate the manifest, revision, or membership rule before reading a corpus-wide count or coverage claim.
public_glossary.scope_note: A corpus result covers that corpus and nothing outside it.
public_glossary.short_definition: A corpus is a fixed body of material treated as one collection, so results can be quoted against a known set rather than an open-ended one.

public_glossary.card_definition: Software correctness relates behaviour to a specification, mathematical correctness relates reasoning to accepted rules and premises, and factual correctness relates a claim to reality. Each requires its own evidence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Local correctness does not automatically compose into whole-system correctness because interactions, assumptions, and uncovered conditions can introduce failure.
public_glossary.example: A generated page is structurally correct when it satisfies the builder's schema and link rules.
public_glossary.label: correctness
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Passing one test does not establish correctness outside that test's coverage.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Correctness is the property of satisfying the specification, rule, or truth condition relevant to the thing being judged.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a correctness claim together with the standard and scope against which it was established.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers bounded claims about software, mathematics, data, and documentation.
public_glossary.short_definition: Correctness is the property of satisfying the specification, rule, or truth condition relevant to the thing being judged.

public_glossary.card_definition: Counts look simple but depend on what qualifies as one item, how duplicates are handled, and which period or source is included. Those rules determine whether two counts are comparable.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A precise count can still answer the wrong question if the collection omits relevant items or combines unlike units.
public_glossary.example: The registry count is the number of unique term rows in the JSON collection.
public_glossary.label: count
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: The byte size of a file is not its count of glossary entries.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A count is the number of items, events, or occurrences in a defined collection or measurement boundary.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read every reported count with its unit, inclusion rules, and measurement boundary.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers totals reported for terms, pages, links, tests, artifacts, and evidence events.
public_glossary.short_definition: A count is the number of items, events, or occurrences in a defined collection or measurement boundary.

public_glossary.card_definition: The asymmetry is total: proving a general claim requires covering every case, while refuting it requires exactly one. Several results here work by narrowing what a surviving counterexample would have to look like, which is progress even when none is found, because each constraint shrinks where one could hide.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Narrowing is the usual shape of progress on a problem that resists both proof and refutation: the space of possible failures gets smaller without closing.
public_glossary.example: After the #243 exclusions, a surviving counterexample must have unbounded negative excursions and divergent normalised negative mass.
public_glossary.label: counterexample
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A counterexample is a single case that fails a general statement, which is enough to disprove it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A constraint on counterexamples is a real result even when no counterexample exists.
public_glossary.scope_note: A constraint covers the properties it derives, not the existence question.
public_glossary.short_definition: A counterexample is a single case that fails a general statement, which is enough to disprove it.

public_glossary.card_definition: Coverage is meaningful only when the denominator is named. A count of linked declarations, tested routes, or reviewed claims can show completeness inside a known inventory while saying nothing about objects that were never included in that inventory.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A coverage receipt pairs the numerator with the authoritative inventory and the method used to match items, preventing a large count from masquerading as completeness over an undefined universe.
public_glossary.example: The semantic corpus reports how many declarations are linked to statement nodes and how many remain orphaned.
public_glossary.label: coverage
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Coverage here is a numerator measured against a named inventory, matching method, and time; it is not correctness, completeness over an unknown universe, or a generic test-coverage percentage.
public_glossary.non_example: A high coverage percentage does not establish correctness of the covered items or completeness beyond the declared inventory.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Coverage is the measured portion of a declared population, surface, or requirement set that a process has actually inspected, represented, or satisfied.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask what the total population is, how membership was determined, and what uncovered items remain.
public_glossary.scope_note: Coverage applies to one declared inventory, method, and measurement time.
public_glossary.short_definition: Coverage is the measured portion of a declared population, surface, or requirement set that a process has actually inspected, represented, or satisfied.

public_glossary.card_definition: Critic posture is one of the system's named judgment traits, used when people and an agent are working an idea out together. Instead of agreeing and moving on, it pauses to test the idea: it names the candidate term being introduced, checks whether the system can actually route to it, and asks what a newcomer would miss. When a criticism holds up under that test, it is not left as a passing remark; it is turned into something durable, such as a refined definition, a recorded rule, or a standard.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Its characteristic move is the failure question: what would a fresh reader miss here, which route currently fails, which standard is absent, or which single case is being treated as a general rule. A criticism that stays stable is then converted into a governed artifact rather than remaining a chat objection.
public_glossary.example: The Routing Anti Patterns Registry is a concrete result of critic posture: a recorded set of failure modes, each one a criticism that held up under testing and was written down as a durable rule rather than left as a passing objection.

example_route.gloss: open the recorded failure modes that stabilized criticism produces
example_route.label: Routing Anti Patterns Registry

public_glossary.label: critic posture
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Critic posture is the Type A practice of stress-testing an abstraction, route, or missing standard and durably recording what survives; it is not negativity, a reviewer identity, or a free-floating opinion.
public_glossary.non_example: Critic posture is not a separate reviewer role that must be spawned, and it is not a judgment that the whole system is flawed. It is the habit of testing one idea at its weak points and recording what holds.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Critic posture is a repeatable way of testing an emerging idea by asking which abstraction is weak, which route has no answer, and which governing standard is missing, rather than offering a one-off objection.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When you meet critic posture on this site, read it as the discipline of pressing on an idea's weak points and then recording what survives, not as a separate reviewer or a verdict on the whole system.

relationships.gloss: Critic posture is one Type A judgment trait.
The move is expressed through repeatable skills before becoming adapter prose.
Critic posture checks whether common sense has a routeable artifact outcome.
Stable critique becomes durable by up-propagating to the owning plane.

public_glossary.scope_note: Critic posture covers the judgment trait applied during human and agent brainstorming, where ideas are stress-tested before they become doctrine. A reader meets it in the doctrine and agent-reliability material, and sees its results in the recorded rules and anti-patterns that stabilized criticism produces.
public_glossary.short_definition: Critic posture is a repeatable way of testing an emerging idea by asking which abstraction is weak, which route has no answer, and which governing standard is missing, rather than offering a one-off objection.

source_refs.gloss: Thinking-session workflow where critic posture becomes a repeatable move.
Plane-home and route-gap repair lane for critique that stabilizes.
Keeps critic posture boot-visible as a pointer, not adapter philosophy.
Shared grammar where the trait is governed.

public_glossary.card_definition: Data can be measured, declared, copied, computed, or generated, and those origins affect what it can support. Structure makes data easier to validate but does not make it correct.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The same facts can appear in raw observations, normalized records, indexes, and presentation projections, so provenance is needed to avoid counting copies as independent evidence.
public_glossary.example: A JSON result file contains structured data about one check run.
public_glossary.label: data
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A confident narrative with no inspectable values is not a dataset.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Data is recorded information represented in a form that people or programs can store, inspect, and process.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask where the data came from, how it was transformed, and which schema and version apply.
public_glossary.scope_note: Data covers the values, representation, source, and collection conditions stated for the artifact.
public_glossary.short_definition: Data is recorded information represented in a form that people or programs can store, inspect, and process.

public_glossary.card_definition: A dataset needs a description of its membership, source, format, collection process, and known limitations. Size alone does not establish representativeness or quality.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Splits, filtering, deduplication, labels, and later corrections can materially change what a dataset supports even when its name remains the same.
public_glossary.example: A fixture dataset may contain the committed cases used by one validator test.
public_glossary.label: dataset
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Several unrelated files in one directory do not automatically form a coherent dataset.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A dataset is an identified collection of related data records assembled for analysis, testing, training, or reference.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the dataset's provenance and sampling boundary before generalizing from it.
public_glossary.scope_note: A dataset covers the records and version included by its manifest or collection rule.
public_glossary.short_definition: A dataset is an identified collection of related data records assembled for analysis, testing, training, or reference.

public_glossary.card_definition: A decision should name what was chosen, why, who or what had authority, and what evidence was considered. It can later be reviewed without pretending it was an objective fact.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Separating decisions from observations prevents policy choices and judgment calls from being smuggled into the system as if they were measurements.
public_glossary.example: A release decision may permit publishing one checked artifact while withholding another.
public_glossary.label: decision
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A measurement or test result is not a decision until an authorized rule interprets it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A decision is a recorded choice among alternatives that determines a status, route, permission, or next action.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a decision together with its authority, rationale, and consequences.
public_glossary.scope_note: A decision governs the alternatives and downstream actions named in its record.
public_glossary.short_definition: A decision is a recorded choice among alternatives that determines a status, route, permission, or next action.

public_glossary.card_definition: It is the unit the Lean corpus is counted in. Declarations are not equally interesting: one may be a substantial theorem and the next a mechanical step generated in bulk, and a count that does not separate them will mislead. That is why the corpus is reported both as raw declarations and as the far smaller number of distinct statements they reduce to.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Counting declarations is the easiest metric to inflate and the least informative to inflate, because generated steps are cheap. The interesting figure is what survives deduplication.
public_glossary.example: The corpus holds 153,238 declarations, which reduce to 6,036 distinct statements.
public_glossary.label: declaration
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A declaration is one named item in a proof library: a single theorem, definition or structure, as written in the source.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A declaration count measures size, not content. Ask how many distinct statements it reduces to.
public_glossary.scope_note: A declaration establishes what it states, once checked.
public_glossary.short_definition: A declaration is one named item in a proof library: a single theorem, definition or structure, as written in the source.

public_glossary.card_definition: A declaration makes a fact inspectable and checkable by giving it a named field or row. It improves accountability, but it does not make the statement true merely because someone wrote it down; evidence and validation still have to support it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Declarations are useful because disagreement becomes visible: a builder can compare a declared source hash, status, scope, or dependency with the state it recomputes and fail when the two diverge.
public_glossary.example: A component declares which fixtures it reads and which claims its result is allowed to support.
public_glossary.label: declare
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A value inferred from a filename or surrounding prose has not been declared.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To declare something is to state its value, status, dependency, or boundary explicitly in the governing data instead of leaving it to inference.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a declared value as explicit input to a check, not as proof that the value is correct.
public_glossary.scope_note: A declaration covers the exact field, row, or contract in which the statement is made.
public_glossary.short_definition: To declare something is to state its value, status, dependency, or boundary explicitly in the governing data instead of leaving it to inference.

public_glossary.card_definition: A useful definition is self-contained enough for a cold reader and precise enough to distinguish the term from its siblings. It does not merely repeat the word or list examples.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Definitions on this site are governed projections: they help readers interpret the public material but defer factual authority to the sources and records they describe.
public_glossary.example: The definition of evidence says both what can support a claim and why a repeated assertion cannot.
public_glossary.label: definition
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: “A record is something recorded” is circular wording, not a useful definition.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A definition states what a term means in a particular context and which nearby meanings it excludes.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use the definition to identify the concept, then read its scope and non-example to find the boundary.
public_glossary.scope_note: A definition governs the term within the context and version that publishes it.
public_glossary.short_definition: A definition states what a term means in a particular context and which nearby meanings it excludes.

public_glossary.card_definition: If an infinite sum turns out to be rational, it has an exact denominator, and that single number constrains everything about it. Several results here work by showing what the denominator would have to be and then showing no such number can exist, which is why so much of the argument is about denominators rather than about the sum.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The denominator is the handle rationality gives you. It is the reason assuming rationality is productive: it converts an infinite object into a finite one you can reason about.
public_glossary.example: For a finite support, the reduced denominator has multiplicative order exactly the least common multiple of the support.
public_glossary.label: denominator
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The denominator is the bottom number of a fraction, the one you are dividing by.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A statement about a possible denominator is a statement about whether the value can be rational at all.
public_glossary.scope_note: A denominator constraint covers the value it is derived for.
public_glossary.short_definition: The denominator is the bottom number of a fraction, the one you are dividing by.

public_glossary.card_definition: Undeclared dependencies are the usual reason something works for its author and fails for everyone else: the author's machine already had it. Declaring them is what makes a cold clone meaningful, and a probe that checks them before anything else is what turns a confusing failure into a clear one.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The failure this prevents is silent rather than loud. An undeclared dependency does not announce itself; it simply makes the published thing work for exactly one person.
public_glossary.example: The pre-install probe reports missing dependencies before any component runs.
public_glossary.label: dependency
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A dependency is other software a project needs in order to run, which must be installed before its checks will work.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check that dependencies are declared before treating a project as runnable.
public_glossary.scope_note: Declared dependencies cover what the project knows it needs.
public_glossary.short_definition: A dependency is other software a project needs in order to run, which must be installed before its checks will work.

public_glossary.card_definition: Deployment moves a verified build into a live location and then checks that the served bytes match the intended output. It does not by itself approve the product, prove the content correct, or establish that every route works in every client.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A reliable deployment binds the source revision, generated output, destination, content hashes, and post-publish probes so a later reader can distinguish successful publication from a command that merely exited without error.
public_glossary.example: The public-site deploy publishes the generated Plectis files and verifies their hashes at the live host.
public_glossary.label: deployment
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A local build or committed change is not a deployment.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A deployment is the act and recorded result of publishing a built artifact to the environment where its intended readers or users can access it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat deployed as an availability state and look for a separate live-verification receipt before assuming the intended build is being served.
public_glossary.scope_note: A deployment covers the named output, destination, revision, and verification time.
public_glossary.short_definition: A deployment is the act and recorded result of publishing a built artifact to the environment where its intended readers or users can access it.

public_glossary.card_definition: Derivations occur in mathematics, logic, data processing, and generated systems. Each step should follow an allowed rule so the result can be traced back to its premises or inputs.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A derivation explains how a result follows; it does not by itself show that the starting assumptions accurately describe the intended real-world subject.
public_glossary.example: A generated page has a derivation from registry data through the deterministic site builder.
public_glossary.label: derivation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A result asserted without intermediate rules or a reproducible procedure is not an inspectable derivation.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A derivation is an ordered sequence of valid transformations or inferences that obtains a result from stated starting material.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check a derivation by examining its starting assumptions, transformation rules, intermediate steps, and final result.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers proof calculations, formula transformations, and source-to-projection computation chains.
public_glossary.short_definition: A derivation is an ordered sequence of valid transformations or inferences that obtains a result from stated starting material.

public_glossary.card_definition: Design connects purposes to choices. It includes trade-offs among usability, correctness, maintainability, cost, safety, and other requirements rather than appearance alone.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A design can be coherent yet based on wrong requirements, so intent, implementation, and observed outcome must remain distinguishable.
public_glossary.example: Making first-use glossary cues faint while preserving focus visibility is an interface design choice.
public_glossary.label: design
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A colour preference without a purpose or constraint is not a complete design rationale.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Design is the intentional shaping of something's structure, behaviour, appearance, or use to satisfy stated goals and constraints.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Evaluate a design by the goals and constraints it addresses and by evidence from its actual use.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers software, interface, information, and workflow design represented on the site.
public_glossary.short_definition: Design is the intentional shaping of something's structure, behaviour, appearance, or use to satisfy stated goals and constraints.

public_glossary.card_definition: Determinism makes a result easier to reproduce and compare because changes in output can be attributed to changed inputs or code. The claim must name the relevant environment, since clocks, network responses, dependency versions, and unordered data can otherwise reintroduce variation.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Determinism is a property of the transformation under a specified boundary, not a promise that the transformation is correct or that every external system it calls will behave consistently.
public_glossary.example: Generating the glossary twice from the same registry and builder revision should produce byte-identical output.
public_glossary.label: deterministic
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A process is not deterministic merely because two observed runs happened to agree.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Deterministic means the same declared inputs and environment produce the same output and decision every time, without hidden randomness or external variation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a process is called deterministic, check which inputs and environmental conditions are fixed.
public_glossary.scope_note: Deterministic applies to the named process under its declared inputs, versions, and environment.
public_glossary.short_definition: Deterministic means the same declared inputs and environment produce the same output and decision every time, without hidden randomness or external variation.

public_glossary.card_definition: Diagrams compress relationships that may be hard to scan in prose. Their labels and edges are selective, so the source graph or text remains necessary for exact membership and semantics.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A generated diagram can remain synchronized with structured source, while a hand-drawn diagram needs an explicit maintenance and freshness claim.
public_glossary.example: An architecture diagram can show how the public pages, records, and source files connect.
public_glossary.label: diagram
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A decorative image with no encoded relationship is not a system diagram.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A diagram is a visual representation that uses spatial arrangement, shapes, and connections to explain structure or relationships.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a diagram for orientation and follow its legend and source pointers for precision.
public_glossary.scope_note: A diagram covers the objects and relationships intentionally included in its visual frame.
public_glossary.short_definition: A diagram is a visual representation that uses spatial arrangement, shapes, and connections to explain structure or relationships.

public_glossary.card_definition: Digests are how this site checks that a published copy really matches its source: the deploy compares the digest of every paper against the public repository before it will publish, and refuses if any differ. A digest proves sameness cheaply and exactly, which is worth more than a promise that nothing changed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This is the precise limit of digest-based evidence, and the reason components carry source bodies rather than only hashes: identical bytes can still be the wrong bytes.
public_glossary.example: The deploy verifies the live stylesheet's digest before reporting success.
public_glossary.label: digest
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A digest is a short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, used to check that two copies are byte-for-byte identical.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A matching digest proves the bytes are identical. It proves nothing about whether they are right.
public_glossary.scope_note: A digest establishes byte identity between two copies.
public_glossary.short_definition: A digest is a short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, used to check that two copies are byte-for-byte identical.

public_glossary.card_definition: Directories organize location and ownership but do not by themselves state the meaning of their contents. A repository convention or index explains what belongs there.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Renaming or moving a directory changes paths and can break references even when the contained files are unchanged.
public_glossary.example: `sites/microcosm/docs` is the directory containing generated documentation pages.
public_glossary.label: directory
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A conceptual category on a web page is not necessarily a filesystem directory.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A directory is a named container in a filesystem that groups files and other directories under one path.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use the directory path to locate files and the governing documentation to understand their roles.
public_glossary.scope_note: A directory covers the filesystem entries directly or recursively contained at its named path, as the context specifies.
public_glossary.short_definition: A directory is a named container in a filesystem that groups files and other directories under one path.

public_glossary.card_definition: A disclosure can reveal limitations, interests, provenance, risks, or previously private facts. Good disclosure identifies what is being revealed, to whom, and for what decision.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Transparency depends on relevance and clarity, not merely on publishing a large volume of material.
public_glossary.example: A page that states its evidence boundary makes a disclosure about what readers may infer.
public_glossary.label: disclosure
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A vague claim that everything is transparent is not a specific disclosure.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Disclosure is the act or result of making relevant information visible to an intended audience.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a disclosure as bounded information and do not infer that unmentioned matters were also examined or released.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers public statements that expose provenance, limitations, relationships, or risk.
public_glossary.short_definition: Disclosure is the act or result of making relevant information visible to an intended audience.

public_glossary.card_definition: Its subjects include combinatorics, graph theory, logic, algorithms, and many parts of number theory. Discrete does not mean small: an infinite set can still have discrete structure.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Computer science and formal proof frequently use discrete mathematics because symbolic states and program steps can be represented as countable structures.
public_glossary.example: Integers and finite graphs are standard objects of discrete mathematics.
public_glossary.label: discrete mathematics
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A problem about a continuously varying physical field is not discrete merely because a computer samples it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Discrete mathematics studies structures made of distinct, separately countable objects rather than continuously varying quantities.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Look for individually distinguishable objects and exact relations rather than continuous change.
public_glossary.scope_note: Discrete mathematics covers the discrete objects and relations named by the problem or theory.
public_glossary.short_definition: Discrete mathematics studies structures made of distinct, separately countable objects rather than continuously varying quantities.

public_glossary.card_definition: Divergence is relative to a specified mode of convergence: values may grow without bound, oscillate, or fail to settle for another reason. The reason matters to later arguments.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A divergent series can still have meaningful partial sums, transformed expressions, or alternative summation methods, but those are not ordinary convergence.
public_glossary.example: If partial sums grow without bound, the series diverges in the ordinary sense.
public_glossary.label: divergence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: A slowly converging sequence is not divergent merely because a finite computation has not reached its limit.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Divergence means that a sequence, series, or limiting process does not approach a finite limit in the stated sense.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the object and definition of convergence before reading a divergence claim.
public_glossary.scope_note: Divergence covers the exact sequence, series, parameter, and convergence notion named by the statement.
public_glossary.short_definition: Divergence means that a sequence, series, or limiting process does not approach a finite limit in the stated sense.

public_glossary.card_definition: The notation d ∣ n means that d divides n with no remainder. Divisibility is an exact integer relation, not an approximate numerical one.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Divisors organize factorisation, primality, congruences, and multiplicative functions such as Euler's totient. Distinguishing positive, negative, proper, and unit divisors is therefore a theorem-level convention, not cosmetic notation.
public_glossary.example: 3 is a divisor of 12 because 12 = 3 × 4.
public_glossary.label: divisor
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: 5 is not a divisor of 12 because no integer multiplied by 5 equals 12.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An integer divisor of an integer n is an integer d for which n equals d times another integer.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the domain and whether zero or negative divisors are included by the convention in use.
public_glossary.scope_note: Divisor covers the integer relation and conventions stated in the surrounding theorem or definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An integer divisor of an integer n is an integer d for which n equals d times another integer.

public_glossary.card_definition: Documentation supplies orientation, examples, and routes through the underlying material. Some docs are authored and some are generated, so a reader should check the page's source and freshness before treating a current detail as settled.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Documentation is a reading surface rather than one evidence class: a page may faithfully project live data, summarize a stable rule, or simply explain how to run a command, and those roles carry different authority.
public_glossary.example: The quickstart docs explain how to clone the repository and run the first check.
public_glossary.label: docs
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Docs are not automatically the source of truth for generated counts, live status, or proof claims.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Docs are human-readable explanations and instructions that help a reader understand or use the system without replacing the source files, records, or contracts they describe.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use docs to understand and navigate, then follow their source references for authority-sensitive claims.
public_glossary.scope_note: Docs cover the explanations and instructions contained on their stated page or document version.
public_glossary.short_definition: Docs are human-readable explanations and instructions that help a reader understand or use the system without replacing the source files, records, or contracts they describe.

public_glossary.card_definition: Doctrine is not one document but a network of governed artifacts: principles, anti-patterns, concepts, mechanisms, standards, and recorded lessons, each given a name and a place. It captures the operating theory of the system, the rules it holds itself to and the ideas it is built around, so that the reasoning behind a design is written down rather than left implicit. Each piece can be opened on its own and traced back to the source it came from.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Doctrine entries come in kinds, including axioms the system takes as given, principles it follows, anti-patterns it forbids, and concepts and mechanisms it names; together they form the meaning lattice the rest of the system is read against.
public_glossary.example: The axiom "Derivation before assertion", which holds that a claim should be derived from evidence before it is stated as fact, is one doctrine card: a single named principle in the doctrine layer with its own entry on the Doctrine page.

example_route.gloss: browse the curated doctrine cards
example_route.label: Derivation before assertion

public_glossary.label: doctrine
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Doctrine names this repository's curated principle-concept-mechanism layer. It is not religious, legal, military, or generally authoritative doctrine outside the system.
public_glossary.non_example: Doctrine is not the source code or the running machinery, and it is not a binding guarantee that the system behaves as described. It is the recorded set of principles and ideas the system is meant to follow, which the components and checks are responsible for actually enforcing.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Doctrine is the curated, searchable layer of principles, concepts, mechanisms, routes, and interpretations that explains why the system is shaped as it is, distinct from the code that implements those ideas.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a doctrine entry as a statement of intent and principle, not as proof that the running code obeys it. It tells you what the system means to do and why; the matching component or check is where that intent is actually carried out.

relationships.gloss: Principles are doctrine nodes.
Concepts are doctrine nodes.
Mechanisms are doctrine nodes.

public_glossary.scope_note: Doctrine covers the explicit-meaning layer of the system and is encountered on the Doctrine page and its individual cards, with cross-references reaching into components, paper modules, and the standards they enforce.
public_glossary.short_definition: Doctrine is the curated, searchable layer of principles, concepts, mechanisms, routes, and interpretations that explains why the system is shaped as it is, distinct from the code that implements those ideas.

source_refs.gloss: Root ontology paper module.

public_glossary.card_definition: Downloading changes where a copy is stored, not where its authority originates. The local copy can become stale or be modified independently after transfer.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A download provides possession of bytes under available permissions; it does not by itself verify authenticity or safety.
public_glossary.example: A reader can download a PDF paper to read it offline.
public_glossary.label: download
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.non_example: Opening a web page in a browser is not necessarily the same as intentionally downloading its offered artifact.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A download transfers a copy of data or a file from a remote service to a reader's device or local environment.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the source, file type, version, integrity, and license before relying on a download.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers public files and data intentionally offered for local retrieval.
public_glossary.short_definition: A download transfers a copy of data or a file from a remote service to a reader's device or local environment.

public_glossary.card_definition: Drift is quiet by construction. Nothing errors; a stale page simply carries an old number with the same confidence as a current one, and a reader has no way to tell. This is why so much of the site is a projection with a build that fails when its output no longer matches its source. Drift caught by a build is a broken build; drift caught by a reader is a broken claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The dangerous case is a hand-edited copy that is more current than its source, because regenerating destroys the correction and looks like a fix. Keeping authorship in one place is what makes drift recoverable.
public_glossary.example: The import-drift area collects components that check whether copied bodies still match the source they were taken from.
public_glossary.label: drift
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Drift is divergence between a generated projection and the source authority that owns its claim; it does not mean every gradual change, model drift, or ordinary project evolution.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Drift is the gap that opens when a generated surface stops matching the source it was generated from, so a page, count, or copy keeps reporting something that is no longer true.
public_glossary.reader_rule: If two surfaces disagree, suspect drift and find the source authority before believing either.
public_glossary.scope_note: Drift detection covers the surfaces a build actually regenerates. Anything outside that set can be stale without being noticed.
public_glossary.short_definition: Drift is the gap that opens when a generated surface stops matching the source it was generated from, so a page, count, or copy keeps reporting something that is no longer true.

Grounds this Plectis-specific definition and its scope.

public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis keeps the first view deliberately small, then lets the selected object open through progressively richer bands: a glossary definition can open its contextual card and scope, an option row can open its source-backed card, and a paper-module summary can open the module itself. A valid drilldown preserves the object’s stable identity and moves closer to its evidence or owner; it does not merely send the reader to another page mentioning the same words.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Drilldown is a depth transition, not an authority promotion. The summary remains a projection, while the destination contributes whatever authority its own contract grants. Stable ids and source references are therefore part of the operation: without them, a deeper-looking page may silently change subjects.
public_glossary.example: Selecting a paper-module card and opening its source view is a drilldown.
public_glossary.label: drilldown
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A drilldown opens greater depth for the same identified object and should preserve its source route; an arbitrary related link is navigation, not a drilldown.
public_glossary.non_example: A link to an unrelated page is navigation, not a drilldown into the selected subject.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A drilldown is a route from a summary or aggregate view into more specific underlying detail.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a drilldown when the summary no longer answers the question, and verify that the deeper surface refers to the same identified object.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers links and commands that open a selected row, component, module, or evidence record in greater detail.
public_glossary.short_definition: A drilldown is a route from a summary or aggregate view into more specific underlying detail.
